{{Short description|American physicist and businessman (1928–2013)}}{{Use American English|date=May 2026}}

{{Use mdy dates|date=May 2026}}
{{for|the British priest|Richard Seed (priest)}}
'''Richard Griffith Seed''' (May 22, 1928 – November 17, 2013) was an American physicist and businessman best known for forcing a national debate on [[human cloning]] in the late 1990s.<ref name="bonnicken2002">Bonnicksen, Andrea L. 2002. Crafting a Cloning Policy: From Dolly to Stem Cells. Washington, DC: Georgetown University Press.</ref>

==Life and career==
Seed was born in [[Chicago, Illinois]] on May 22, 1928. He graduated from [[Oak Park and River Forest High School]] in Illinois before attending [[Harvard University]], earning his undergraduate degree there in 1949.<ref name="crimson1998">Staff report (September 14, 1998). [http://www.thecrimson.com/article/1998/9/14/seed-proposes-cloning-himself-pa-controversial/ Seed Proposes Cloning Himself] ''[[Harvard Crimson]]''</ref> He later received a master's degree, as well as a Ph.D. in physics from Harvard in 1953. His interests soon shifted to the new frontier of [[biomedicine]]. In the 1970s, Seed co-founded a company that commercialized a technique for transferring embryos in cattle. Later, he and his brother, Chicago surgeon Randolph Seed, started another company, Fertility & Genetics Research Inc., to help infertile women conceive children using the same technique.<ref name="evans2000">Evans, Debra (2000). ''Without Moral Limits: Women, Reproduction, and Medical Technology.'' Crossway, {{ISBN|9781581342017}}</ref> These efforts to transplant a [[human embryo]] from one woman to an infertile [[surrogate mother]] were published in 1984. The cumbersome procedure involved flushing embryos out of the [[uterus]] of the egg donor and was soon eclipsed by [[in-vitro fertilization]]. Ultimately, the venture failed.

On December 5, 1997, Seed announced that he planned to clone a human being before any federal laws could be enacted to ban the process.<ref name="nyt1998">{{cite news|url=https://www.nytimes.com/1998/01/24/us/eccentric-s-hubris-set-off-global-frenzy-over-cloning.html|title=Eccentric's Hubris Set Off Global Frenzy Over Cloning|first=Dirk|last=Johnson|date=January 24, 1998|via=NYTimes.com}}</ref> Seed's announcement added fuel to the raging ethical debate on human cloning that had been sparked by [[Ian Wilmut]]'s creation of [[Dolly the sheep]], the first clone obtained from adult cells.<ref name="pbs">{{cite web |url=http://www.pbs.org/newshour/bb/science/jan-june98/cloning_1-8.html |title=Online NewsHour: Human Cloning -- January 8, 1998 |website=www.pbs.org |access-date=15 January 2022 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/19990117003642/http://www.pbs.org/newshour/bb/science/jan-june98/cloning_1-8.html |archive-date=17 January 1999 |url-status=dead}}</ref> Seed's plans were to use the same technique used by the Scottish team.<ref name="scifri">{{cite web |url=http://www.sciencefriday.com/pages/1998/Jan/hour1_010998.html |title=January 9, 1998, Hour 1: Human Cloning |website=www.sciencefriday.com |access-date=15 January 2022 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/19980131071704/http://www.sciencefriday.com/pages/1998/Jan/hour1_010998.html |archive-date=31 January 1998 |url-status=dead}}</ref> Seed's announcement went against President Clinton's 1997 proposal for a voluntary private moratorium against human cloning. In the media frenzy that followed, the story of a 69-year-old eccentric maverick scientist emerged, but Seed possessed impressive credentials and was not dismissed immediately.<ref name="cnn">{{cite news|url=http://www.cnn.com/TECH/9801/07/cloning.folo/|title=CNN - Opposition to human cloning will 'blow over,' scientist says - January 7, 1998|website=www.cnn.com}}</ref> While virtually no mainstream scientist believed Seed would succeed, there began a subtle shift in attitudes after Seed made his announcement.<ref name="merrill2011">Merrill, Richard A.; Rose, Bryan J. FDA Regulation of Human Cloning: Usurpation or Statesmanship; 15 [[Harv. J. L. Tech]] 85: (2001-2002)</ref>

Although he was retired at the time of his announcement to clone the first human, Seed was reported to have dabbled in other ill-fated ventures in the past. He claimed, at one time, to have commitments for $800,000 toward a goal of $2.5 million needed to clone the first human before the year 2000. Seed first said that he was going to make little baby clones{{cn|date=October 2026}} for infertile couples. Later, "to defuse criticism that I'm taking advantage of desperate women," he announced that he would first clone himself. He later announced that he would re-create his wife Gloria. "God made man in his own image," he told National Public Radio correspondent [[Joe Palca]] in December 1997. He also stated that "God intended for man to become one with God”, and that cloning is the “first serious step in becoming one with God". In a later interview on CNN, Seed elaborated: "Man," he said, "will develop the technology and the science and the capability to have an indefinite life span".{{cn|date=October 2026}}

In 1998, the [[Ig Nobel Prize]] in economics,<ref>{{Cite web|url=https://www.improbable.com/ig-about/winners/#ig1998|title=Past Ig Winners|date=August 2006}}</ref> a satirical version of the [[Nobel Memorial Prize in Economics]], was awarded to Seed, for which a performance titled ''The Seedy Opera'' was held.<ref name="Wickramasekara">Wickramasekara, Sagara (October 5, 1999). [http://tech.mit.edu/V119/N47/47ignobel2.47n.html Not-so-noble Prizes Amuse and Bemuse Audiences.] ''[[The Tech (newspaper)|The Tech]]''</ref>

Richard Seed died in [[Hobart, Indiana]] on November 17, 2013, at the age of 85.<ref>{{cite web |title=Richard G. Seed |url=https://www.ancestry.co.uk/discoveryui-content/view/5176601:60716?tid=&pid=&queryId=5475ca3dccefd79ef48603d8b34a9f98&_phsrc=Dqh6510&_phstart=successSource |publisher=Indiana, U.S., Death Certificates, 1899–2017 |access-date=14 November 2023}}</ref>
